When learning a new game, do you prefer the manual, videos or being taught by someone who already knows?

If I had to choose one, it would be the manual, that way there is no ambiguity. When a game is being explained by someone else they may phrase something in a slightly different way or forget to mention some minor rule and you may end up with a different idea of how the game is played. With the manual you know exactly what the rules are and you know all the rules from the start without any need for clarification later.

This in combination with somebody who already knows explaining it, however, can be better as they can tell you about strategies or little tricks that aren't in the manual. If you first read the manual to learn the rules and then have someone else explain the game further you get a better understanding of what the best way to play is, so I prefer this method.
Manual or video. For some reason, those who know the rules tend to focus on fringe cases or strategy as opposed to game structure.

I have to admit myself, while I enjoy videos for getting the 'feel' of a game and I don't mind being taught, there's something very visceral and gritty about that manual. Particularly if it's well written, which can be a hit or miss thing.

I love getting down with the book, the game and a good 45 minutes alone at my dining room table. It is for me almost as much fun as playing the game with other people. That way I can really get a feel for how everything works and also I get to inhale a bit of the off-gassing from those new cards. That new game smell!

I prefer to learn by playing. When the game forces a player to use a feature to progress, it feels far more natural and intuitive. A good example of this is Megaman X. This game teaches you how to play through level design of the intro.

It really depends on the game. If there's a good video like the Watch It Played intro/rules videos those are a pretty great starting point.

After that I'll probably check through the manual for specifics. Some games are simple enough that a quick read through the manual tells you everything you need to know... others have so many mechanics in play at the same time that it can be a bit of a mess reading through the manual so having a visual reference (video) breaking down the game is really helpful.

I get bored reading, and I'm usually fidgeting with components while someone is explaining the game. Watching videos mostly does the trick for me. There are some really good series out there, Dice Tower, Table Top, and BGG Game Night! seem to fill all my instructional needs.

Thanks to youtube I now prefer watching a video of a game first before reading the rulebook. As a matter of fact I just finished a weekend of gaming with some buddies and we played a new game(to us) Castles of Burgundy. As none of us had ever played the game before the first thing we did was watch a gameplay video before even opening the box. It made the first game so much easier to set up and play, with less consulting of the rulebook. By the second game we had the rules down pat. And by the third game were able to concentrate on strategy over rules. I also make sure to watch some videos(Tabletop episodes if possible are great for this) of a game before deciding on a purchase.

BTW - Castles of Burgundy is great...I highly recommend.

My friends and I start off with a "dirty play through" and just dive in, looking at the rule book as we go, I would rather learn playing one really crappy round with all types of mistakes. I recommend this to others it makes for a funny first time when we all don't know the game and keep messing up.

Taught by someone who knows. Yes you might pick up "house rules" that way but it seems to expedite the learning curve. Also grew up with pen and paper games where rule were more...guidelines per se. So games were about having fun mostly, making following the rules a secondary action.
I prefer the manual to make sure I get all the correct rules and then look up a video or the internet if I need any clarification

I read the manual first, then I'll watch a video, then I'll reread the manual. Depending on the complexity I'll play a trial game, either by myself or with the girlfriend and then watch the video or read the manual again. Then when I teach the game, I know exactly how to teach it.

Nothing in the article suggests anyone is "livid" or "fuming", which I guess should be expected in a NYPost article.

The fact that anyone is upset over these measures is very suspect. The three the news article mentions are:

Requiring that uniformed cops provide their full name, rank and precinct, as well as the CCRB number, during any traffic stop or property search.

Obviously a good idea. Accountability is important when you're given the legal authority to kill or essentially kidnap (arrest) someone.

A measure that would allow police to use “injurious physical force” only “as is proportionally necessary,” but that does not define how proportionality will be determined.

Hold on, was proportionality not required before? That's always important in civilian cases. It's not phrased that way, but in most states you are only allowed to use lethal force in the face of a force that would reasonably also be called lethal. You cannot shoot someone for throwing sticks at you, but you could shoot someone for trying to stab you. That should always be a requirement in the event that they use lethal force. Let's not forget that they should be trained and armed to use non-lethal force. Pepper spray, tasers and batons are things that police carry that the average citizen would not. Use those unless you fear for your life.

Making the NYPD report the precincts of the 200 cops with the most CCRB complaints filed against them.

Again, I'm surprised this wasn't done before. It's not a good idea to release the names of specific officers, but for statistics purposes it would be a great idea to be able to figure out where most of these violations are occurring. I wish they would release more like the time of the incident, the area of the incident, and age/gender/race of the complainer.
